claims.text: The initial AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles are equiatomic and 3–8 nm in size.
The as-synthesized nanoparticles are a single-phase FCC solid solution.
Rapid quenching or colloidal reduction can kinetically produce the asserted initial mixed state.
Configurational entropy can stabilize a multielement solid solution against phase separation.
The sluggish-diffusion assumption breaks down below a critical particle size of approximately 5 nm.
The sluggish-diffusion assumption breaks down above approximately 600 K, identified as about 0.4 Tm.
Above the proposed thresholds, surface-energy-driven segregation dominates entropy-stabilized kinetics.
Ostwald ripening dominates the structural evolution of the heated nanoparticles.
Au and Cu are the low-surface-energy components in this alloy.
Au and Cu preferentially evaporate or diffuse from small particles to larger particles.
Co, Ni, and Pt preferentially segregate to particle surfaces or form shells.
Coarsening proceeds through a surface-diffusion-limited Ostwald-ripening mechanism rather than sluggish bulk diffusion.
The high surface-to-volume ratio of sub-10 nm particles lowers the activation barrier for surface diffusion.
The thermodynamic drive to minimize surface energy overwhelms entropy stabilization above 600 K.
Particles smaller than 5 nm disappear by dissolution followed by redeposition onto larger particles.
The remaining particles develop Au/Cu-rich cores and Co/Ni/Pt-rich surfaces, or separate into elemental or binary-rich domains.
Heating to 1000 K increases the average particle size by more than 50%.
Heating to 1000 K produces a bimodal particle-size distribution.
Bulk material or particles larger than 20 nm retain a single phase with minimal size change or segregation up to 1000 K because of sluggish diffusion.
An oxidizing atmosphere would alter surface energies and segregation behavior relative to vacuum.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis labels Au and Cu as the low-surface-energy components but sends them away from the surface into the vapor, larger particles, or particle cores, while placing the asserted high-surface-energy Co, Ni, and Pt at the surface. This conflicts with the stated mechanism of minimizing surface energy unless an additional volatility, adsorption, or interfacial-energy argument is supplied.

A sharp breakdown is asserted below about 5 nm, but the boundary states that the hypothesis applies to all particles below 10 nm. The expected regime for particles between 5 and 10 nm is therefore ambiguous.
